claim: Dravet Syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic loss of function variants in the gene SCN1A which encodes the voltage gated sodium (Na+) channel subunit Nav1.1.
source: Dravet Syndrome (DS) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic loss of function variants in the gene SCN1A which encodes the voltage gated sodium (Na+) channel subunit Nav1.1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Dravet Syndrome cited in the abstract and introduction with references to prior literature (Claes et al., 2001).

claim: GABAergic interneurons expressing parvalbumin (PV-INs) and somatostatin (SST-INs) exhibit impaired excitability in DS (Scn1a+/-) mice.
source: GABAergic interneurons expressing parvalbumin (PV-INs) and somatostatin (SST-INs) exhibit impaired excitability in DS (Scn1a+/-) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Favero et al., 2018; Ogiwara et al., 2007; De Stasi et al., 2016; Tai et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2006) mentioned in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Irregular spiking (IS) VIP-INs, but not continuous adapting (CA) VIP-INs, are impaired in Scn1a+/- mice.
source: We recorded VIP-INs in brain slices from Scn1a+/-mice and wild-type littermate controls and found prominent impairment of irregular spiking (IS), but not continuous adapting (CA) VIP-INs, in Scn1a+/- mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Application of the Nav1.1-specific toxin Hm1a rescued the observed deficits in VIP-INs.
source: Application of the Nav1.1-specific toxin Hm1a rescued the observed deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 demonstrating rescue of VIP-IN function with Hm1a application.

claim: The IS vs. CA firing pattern is determined by expression of KCNQ channels.
source: The IS vs. CA firing pattern is determined by expression of KCNQ channels
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments with KCNQ channel modulators shown in Figure 6.

claim: IS VIP-INs switched to tonic firing with pharmacologic blockade of M-current.
source: IS VIP-INs switched to tonic firing with both pharmacologic blockade of M-current and muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with linopirdine application shown in Figure 6.

claim: IS VIP-INs switched to tonic firing with muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation.
source: IS VIP-INs switched to tonic firing with both pharmacologic blockade of M-current and muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with carbachol and muscarine application shown in Figures 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: VIP-INs express Nav1.1.
source: These results show that VIP-INs express Nav1.1 and are dysfunctional in DS
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplements 2-3, as well as transcriptomics data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice demonstrated a reduced maximal steady-state firing frequency (67 ± 2 vs. 48 ± 3 Hz; p=3 X E-6).
source: VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice demonstrated multiple abnormalities that were consistent with loss of Na+ current (Figure 1), including a reduced maximal steady-state firing frequency (67 ± 2 vs. 48 ± 3 Hz; p=3 X E-6; n = 150/123 WT/Scn1a+/-)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice showed a marked shift in the current/frequency (I/f; input-output) curve.
source: VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice demonstrated multiple abnormalities that were consistent with loss of Na+ current (Figure 1), including a reduced maximal steady-state firing frequency (67 ± 2 vs. 48 ± 3 Hz; p=3 X E-6; n = 150/123 WT/Scn1a+/-), as well as a marked shift in the current/frequency (I/f; input-output) curve.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the I-f curves shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice showed spike height accommodation (rundown) during repetitive action potential discharge.
source: There was notable spike height accommodation (rundown) during repetitive action potential discharge with a progressive depolarization of AP threshold and a decrease in AP peak value during suprathreshold current injections, suggesting enhanced accumulation of Na+ channel inactivation in VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and E demonstrating spike amplitude rundown.

claim: 77% of identified VIP-IN axons expressed Nav1.1.
source: We identified the axon in 30 VIP-INs and found that 23 of 30 (77%) identified axons expressed Nav1.1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Approximately half of all VIP-INs fired continuously with spike frequency adaptation (CA VIP-INs), while the other half fired a burst of action potentials prior to switching to an irregular spiking pattern (IS VIP-INs).
source: Approximately half of all VIP-INs fired continuously, albeit with spike frequency adaptation (here referred to as CA VIP-INs), while the other half instead fired a burst of action potentials prior to switching to an irregular spiking pattern (IS VIP-INs), often with a variable silent period in between the two phases (Figure 2A).
evidence: This classification is demonstrated in Figure 2 using k-means clustering and long depolarizations.

claim: CA and IS VIP-INs are present in Scn1a+/- and WT mice in similar proportions.
source: We determined that CA and IS VIP-INs are present in Scn1a+/- and WT mice in similar proportions as determined by our unbiased classification (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 2E with chi-square test p=0.10.

claim: IS VIP-INs displayed a depolarized AP threshold in Scn1a+/- mice compared to WT (−41.3 ± 0.5 vs. −39.3 ± 0.4; p=0.01).
source: IS VIP-INs displayed more severe deficits compared to the pooled dataset (Figure 1), with a depolarized AP threshold (WT vs. Scn1a+/- mice: −41.3 ± 0.5 vs. −39.3 ± 0.4; p=0.01)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: IS VIP-INs displayed decreased AP amplitude in Scn1a+/- mice compared to WT (79 ± 1.0 vs. 72 ± 1.3 mV; p=0.003).
source: IS VIP-INs displayed more severe deficits compared to the pooled dataset (Figure 1), with a depolarized AP threshold (WT vs. Scn1a+/- mice: −41.3 ± 0.5 vs. −39.3 ± 0.4; p=0.01), decreased AP amplitude (79 ± 1.0 vs. 72 ± 1.3 mV; p=0.003)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: IS VIP-INs displayed decreased steady-state firing in Scn1a+/- mice compared to WT (59 ± 4 vs. 25 ± 3 Hz; p=8 X E-9).
source: IS VIP-INs displayed more severe deficits compared to the pooled dataset (Figure 1), with a depolarized AP threshold (WT vs. Scn1a+/- mice: −41.3 ± 0.5 vs. −39.3 ± 0.4; p=0.01), decreased AP amplitude (79 ± 1.0 vs. 72 ± 1.3 mV; p=0.003) and steady-state firing (59 ± 4 vs. 25 ± 3 Hz; p=8 X E-9)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: CA VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice showed no statistical differences compared to CA VIP-INs from age-matched WT littermate controls across a range of measures of intrinsic excitability, properties of individual action potentials, and features of repetitive firing.
source: CA VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice showed no statistical differences compared to CA VIP-INs from age-matched WT littermate controls across a range of additional measures of intrinsic excitability, properties of individual action potentials, and features of repetitive firing (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 and quantified in Table 1.

claim: IS VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice persisted at later developmental time points (P30-55).
source: We subdivided our analysis based on age and found nearly identical results at P18-21 and P30-55 for both IS and CA VIP-INs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 comparing two age groups.

claim: Impairment of IS VIP-INs was observed in both primary somatosensory neocortex and primary visual cortex.
source: To assess whether impairment of IS VIP-INs was a general phenomenon or restricted to primary somatosensory neocortex, we additionally performed a set of recordings in layer 2/3 primary visual cortex, again finding a similar proportion of IS vs. CA VIP-INs and replicating our central finding that IS VIP-INs were selectively hypoexcitable in Scn1a+/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing similar results in visual cortex.

claim: Bath application of 1 µM Hm1a led to markedly increased steady-state firing in IS VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice (control, 33 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 97 ± 5 Hz; p=0.001).
source: In acute brain slices prepared from Scn1a+/- mice, bath application of 1 µM Hm1a led to markedly increased steady-state firing in IS VIP-INs (control, 33 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 97 ± 5 Hz; p=0.001)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacology experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bath application of 1 µM Hm1a led to attenuation of spike rundown in IS VIP-INs from Scn1a+/- mice.
source: In acute brain slices prepared from Scn1a+/- mice, bath application of 1 µM Hm1a led to markedly increased steady-state firing in IS VIP-INs (control, 33 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 97 ± 5 Hz; p=0.001) and attenuation of spike rundown (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C demonstrating reduced spike amplitude rundown with Hm1a.

claim: Hm1a increased the maximum steady-state firing rate of PV-INs in Scn1a+/- mice at P18-21 (control, 229 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 292 ± 6 Hz; p=0.004).
source: As a positive control, Hm1a increased the maximum steady-state firing rate of PV-INs in Scn1a+/- mice at P18-21 (control, 229 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 292 ± 6 Hz; p=0.004)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacology experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hm1a had no measurable effect on the firing of layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons in WT mice.
source: In contrast, Hm1a had no measurable effect on the firing of layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons in WT mice, supporting the specificity of this toxin to Nav1.1 and the smaller role of Nav1.1 in the regulation of pyramidal cell excitability relative to interneurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 demonstrating no effect of Hm1a on pyramidal neurons.

claim: Hm1a slowed the time constant of inactivation and increased slowly-inactivating/persistent current in VIP-INs, with no effect on the peak current density.
source: Hm1a slowed the time constant of inactivation and increased slowly-inactivating/persistent current in VIP-INs, with no effect on the peak current density.
evidence: This is demonstrated in voltage clamp recordings from dissociated VIP-INs shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: CR and CCK did not reliably define electrophysiological subtypes of VIP-INs.
source: VIP/CR-INs were more often bipolar, or 'vertically biased,' compared to VIP/CCK-INs (Figure 5A), as shown previously (He et al., 2016), but CR and CCK did not reliably define electrophysiological subtypes of VIP-INs (Figure 5A–B)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing both CA and IS firing patterns in CR and CCK populations.

claim: There were no differences in morphology between CA and IS VIP-INs within a given genotype.
source: VIP/CR-INs were more often bipolar, or 'vertically biased,' compared to VIP/CCK-INs (Figure 5A), as shown previously (He et al., 2016), but CR and CCK did not reliably define electrophysiological subtypes of VIP-INs (Figure 5A–B), nor were there any differences in morphology between the CA and IS VIP-INs within a given genotype (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D demonstrating similar vertical bias for CA and IS cells within CR and CCK populations.

claim: Kcnq5 was expressed in approximately 40% of layer 2/3 VIP-INs and essentially no SST-INs.
source: Kcnq5 was expressed in ~ 40% of layer 2/3 VIP-INs and essentially no SST-INs (but was expressed in many presumptive pyramidal cells)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kcnq3 showed very limited immunoreactivity in the superficial cortex overall and was not found on VIP-INs.
source: while Kcnq3 showed very limited immunoreactivity in the superficial cortex overall and was not found on VIP-INs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: IS VIP-INs showed a marked increase in sustained firing with the addition of linopirdine and resembled CA VIP-INs in terms of burst length and ISI CoV.
source: IS VIP-INs showed a marked increase in sustained firing with the addition of linopirdine and resembled CA VIP-INs in terms of burst length and ISI CoV.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing conversion of IS to CA-like firing with linopirdine.

claim: Some CA VIP-INs became 'IS-like' upon application of retigabine.
source: Conversely, some CA VIP-INs became 'IS-like' upon application of retigabine.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing conversion of CA to IS-like firing with retigabine.

claim: Linopirdine had essentially no effect on CA VIP-IN excitability or intrinsic properties.
source: However, linopirdine had essentially no effect on CA VIP-IN excitability or intrinsic properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) indicating that whatever M-current is present in these cells is not a major regulator of cellular excitability.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 showing no change in CA VIP-IN properties with linopirdine.

claim: Bath application of carbachol (5 μM) produced a 10–15 mV depolarization in both CA and IS VIP-INs.
source: Bath application of the cholinomimetic carbachol (5 μM) produced a 10–15 mV depolarization in both CA and IS VIP-INs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from pharmacology experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The suprathreshold firing properties of IS VIP-INs converted to a 'CA-like' pattern with carbachol application, firing for a full 8 s depolarizing pulse with decreased irregularity.
source: However, the suprathreshold firing properties of IS VIP-INs again converted to a 'CA-like' pattern, firing for a full 8 s depolarizing pulse with decreased irregularity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7B-C showing conversion of IS to continuous firing with carbachol.

claim: There was essentially no effect of carbachol on the firing pattern of CA VIP-INs.
source: There was essentially no effect on the firing pattern of CA VIP-INs, nor was there any effect on the initial bursting characteristics of either IS or CA VIP-INs (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C demonstrating no change in CA VIP-IN firing patterns with carbachol.

claim: Muscarinic, but not nicotinic stimulation, induced tonic firing in IS VIP-INs.
source: Similarly, we found that muscarinic, but not nicotinic stimulation, induced tonic firing in IS VIP-INs, while both types of cholinergic stimulation independently produced membrane potential depolarization of similar magnitude (4.24 ± 0.7 mV for muscarinic vs. 5.48 ± 1.4 mV for nicotinic; p>0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 comparing muscarinic and nicotinic agonist effects.

claim: PV-IN hypoexcitability in Scn1a+/- mice is restricted to an early and transient developmental window (P11-21), with subsequent normalization of high-frequency action potential discharge by P35.
source: However, we recently showed that PV-IN hypoexcitability in Scn1a+/- mice is restricted to an early and transient developmental window (P11-21), with subsequent normalization of high-frequency action potential discharge by P35 (Favero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by the authors (Favero et al., 2018).

claim: VIP-INs are functionally distinct from SST and PV-INs as they preferentially target other interneurons (particularly SST-INs) rather than pyramidal cells.
source: VIP-INs are functionally distinct from SST and PV-INs as they preferentially target other interneurons (particularly SST-INs) rather than pyramidal cells, and thus are considered to exert a disinhibitory influence on cerebral cortical circuits (Acsády et al., 1998; Fu et al., 2014; Krabbe et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2017; Pi et al., 2013; Turi et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about VIP-IN function supported by multiple citations.

claim: VIP-INs have a role in regulating the response of the cerebral cortex to ascending cholinergic neuromodulatory input from the basal forebrain.
source: VIP-INs also have a role in regulating the response of the cerebral cortex to ascending cholinergic neuromodulatory input from the basal forebrain (Alitto and Dan, 2012; Fu et al., 2015; Kawaguchi, 1997; Porter et al., 1999)
evidence: This is established knowledge about VIP-IN function supported by citations.

claim: VIP-INs are involved in higher-order functions such as attention, memory, and cognitive processing, all of which are impaired in DS.
source: VIP-INs also have a role in regulating the response of the cerebral cortex to ascending cholinergic neuromodulatory input from the basal forebrain (Alitto and Dan, 2012; Fu et al., 2015; Kawaguchi, 1997; Porter et al., 1999), and hence are involved in higher-order functions such as attention, memory, and cognitive processing, all of which are impaired in DS (Dravet and Oguni, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on VIP-IN function and DS symptoms, supported by citation (Dravet and Oguni, 2013).

claim: Prior work has suggested that VIP-INs do not express Nav1.1.
source: Prior work has suggested that VIP-INs do not express Nav1.1 (Yamagata et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a citation to prior work that the current study contradicts.

claim: Recent single cell RNA sequencing studies suggest expression of Nav1.1 in VIP-INs.
source: while recent single cell RNA sequencing studies do suggest expression of Nav1.1 in VIP-INs (Paul et al., 2017; Tasic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomics studies.

claim: Nav1.1 is expressed at the axon initial segment (AIS) of PV-INs and, to a lesser extent, SST-INs.
source: Nav1.1 is expressed at the axon initial segment (AIS) of PV-INs and, to a lesser extent, SST-INs, and is a major determinant of action potential (AP) generation in these cells (Li et al., 2014; Ogiwara et al., 2007; De Stasi et al., 2016; Tai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The 'interneuron hypothesis' of DS posits that PV and SST-IN dysfunction is the predominant driver of both epilepsy and autism.
source: Such data have led to the 'interneuron hypothesis' of DS, which posits that PV and SST-IN dysfunction is the predominant driver of both epilepsy and autism (Catterall, 2018; Catterall et al., 2010; Han et al., 2012; Ogiwara et al., 2007; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of an existing hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Scn1a mRNA is expressed in VIP-INs at levels similar to that seen in SST-INs.
source: However, several recent large-scale transcriptomics datasets suggest that Scn1a mRNA is in fact expressed in VIP-INs, and at levels similar to that seen in SST-INs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Paul et al., 2017; Tasic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited studies.

claim: Hm1a is a spider toxin that enhances Nav1.1 current via inhibiting fast and slow inactivation.
source: Hm1a is a recently described spider toxin that enhances Nav1.1 current via inhibiting fast and slow inactivation (Osteen et al., 2016; Osteen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hm1a supported by citations.

claim: The effect of Hm1a in IS VIP-INs was proportionally larger than in PV-INs (mean difference of 295% in IS VIP-INs compared to 28% in PV-INs).
source: As a positive control, Hm1a increased the maximum steady-state firing rate of PV-INs in Scn1a+/- mice at P18-21 (control, 229 ± 2 Hz; Hm1a, 292 ± 6 Hz; p=0.004), although this effect was proportionally smaller than what we observed in IS VIP INs (mean difference of 295% in IS VIP-INs compared to 28% in PV-INs).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of Hm1a effects between cell types based on data in Figure 4.

claim: IS VIP-INs retain a distinct irregular firing pattern in the presence of Hm1a in response to longer depolarizations.
source: Importantly, although Hm1a causes a dramatic increase in steady-state firing of IS VIP-INs, these cells still retain a distinct irregular firing pattern in the presence of Hm1a in response to longer depolarizations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing irregular firing persists with Hm1a.

claim: M-current is mediated by KCNQ channels and has been hypothesized to regulate mode switching between tonic and bursting/irregular firing.
source: M-current, mediated by KCNQ channels, is known to possess such properties and has been hypothesized to regulate mode switching between tonic and bursting/irregular firing (Drion et al., 2010; Stiefel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M-current supported by citations.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics data suggest relatively high expression of Kcnq5 in a subset of VIP-INs, including approximately half of all VIP/CR and VIP/CCK-INs, with minimal expression in either PV or SST-INs.
source: Single-cell transcriptomics data suggest relatively high expression of the KCNQ subunit Kcnq5 in a subset of VIP-INs, including approximately half of all VIP/CR and VIP/CCK-INs, with minimal expression in either PV or SST-INs.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations (Paul et al., 2017; Tasic et al., 2016).

claim: KCNQ subfamily member Kcnq2 is more broadly expressed across all INs.
source: KCNQ subfamily member Kcnq2 is more broadly expressed across all INs, while Kcnq1/3/4 show very limited cortical expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Paul et al., 2017; Tasic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: M-current expression is a critical but selective determinant of the electrical excitability of IS VIP-INs.
source: Such data indicate that M-current expression is a critical but selective determinant of the electrical excitability of IS VIP-INs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacology experiments with linopirdine and retigabine shown in Figure 6.

claim: M-current does not seem to correlate with expression of VIP-IN markers such as CR and CCK, or with VIP-IN morphology.
source: However, M-current does not seem to correlate with expression of VIP-IN markers such as CR and CCK, or with VIP-IN morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 5 showing no correlation between firing patterns and CR/CCK expression or morphology.

claim: VIP-INs are strongly recruited by ascending cholinergic modulation in vivo.
source: VIP-INs are strongly recruited by ascending cholinergic modulation in vivo (Fu et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: M-current is characteristically inhibited by muscarinic receptor activation.
source: and M-current is characteristically inhibited by muscarinic receptor activation (Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M-current supported by citation.

claim: M-current inhibition via activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors represents a novel mechanism of neuromodulation in VIP-INs that is separate from the recently described tonic depolarization caused by nicotinic acetycholine receptor activation.
source: Hence, M-current inhibition via activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors represents a novel mechanism of neuromodulation in VIP-INs that is separate from the recently described tonic depolarization caused by nicotinic acetycholine receptor activation (Askew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the carbachol and muscarine experiments in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work on nicotinic effects.

claim: A single compartment Hodgkin-Huxley model with M-current recapitulates the CA and IS-VIP firing patterns and the effect of loss of one copy of Scn1a.
source: Therefore, both the CA and IS-VIP firing patterns that characterize VIP-IN diversity, as well as the effect of loss of one copy of Scn1a, are captured in a simple model with continuous distributions of both Na+ and M-current.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model shown in Figure 8.

claim: Most or all VIP-INs express Nav1.1, and IS VIP-INs are selectively dysfunctional in Scn1a+/- mice due to prominent M-current mediated by Kcnq5-containing KCNQ channels.
source: This supports our conclusion that most or all VIP-INs express Nav1.1, and that IS VIP-INs – which have a prominent M-current mediated by Kcnq5-containing KCNQ channels – are selectively dysfunctional in Scn1a+/- mice.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including immunohistochemistry, transcriptomics, pharmacology, and modeling.

claim: VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice is distinct from the time course of PV-IN dysfunction, which is transient and delimited to an early developmental period.
source: This persistent VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice is distinct from the time course of PV-IN dysfunction, which we previously found is transient and delimited to an early developmental period when assessed via the same approach (Favero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work by the authors (Favero et al., 2018) based on the age-dependent data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Seizure frequency typically decreases during early childhood in Dravet syndrome, while cognitive deficits remain, with moderate to severe intellectual disability and features of autism spectrum disorder.
source: Such a time course is consistent with the known natural history of Dravet syndrome in human patients: it is well established that seizure frequency typically decreases during early childhood, while cognitive deficits remain, with moderate to severe intellectual disability and features, or a formal diagnosis of, autism spectrum disorder (Berkvens et al., 2015; Genton et al., 2011; Han et al., 2012; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about Dravet syndrome supported by citations.

claim: Early epilepsy in Dravet syndrome may be driven by transient PV-IN abnormalities while cognitive impairment persists in part due to ongoing VIP-IN hypofunction.
source: it may be the case that early epilepsy in driven by transient PV-IN abnormalities while cognitive impairment persists in part due to ongoing VIP-IN hypofunction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the temporal patterns of PV-IN and VIP-IN dysfunction observed in the study.

claim: VIP-INs are considered to have a role as disinhibitory elements in cortical circuits.
source: As VIP-INs are considered to have a role as disinhibitory elements in cortical circuits
evidence: This is established knowledge about VIP-IN function mentioned earlier with citations.

claim: Brief current pulses on the order of hundreds of milliseconds cannot establish whether a VIP-IN is IS or CA.
source: However, our data clearly indicated that brief current pulses on the order of hundreds of milliseconds (such as are standard in slice physiology experiments) cannot establish whether a VIP-IN is IS or CA, as many IS VIP-INs fire continuously for 600 ms or more prior to transition to an IS pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2 comparing 600 ms and 8 s depolarizations.

claim: Irregular spiking is distinct from, yet partially overlaps with, bursting in VIP-INs.
source: Therefore, irregular spiking is distinct from, yet partially overlaps with, bursting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: T-type calcium channels underlie burst firing in a subset of VIP-INs.
source: A recent study implicated T-type calcium channels as the mechanism of bursting at rheobase observed in a small subset (~20%) of VIP-INs (Prönneke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Prönneke et al., 2018).

claim: A prepulse step depolarization to −55 mV to inactivate T-type channels had no effect on the suprathreshold response of IS-VIPs.
source: A prepulse step depolarization to −55 mV to inactivate T-type channels had no effect on the suprathreshold response of IS-VIPs here (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: CA and IS VIP-INs can be clearly identified using a slow 8 s ramp current injection to induce inactivation of T-type calcium channels.
source: We were able to clearly identify CA and IS VIP-INs using a slow 8 s ramp current injection to induce inactivation of T-type calcium channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: A subset of both CA and IS VIP-INs burst at rheobase.
source: Finally, we found that a subset of both CA and IS VIP-INs burst at rheobase, indicating that our IS VIP-IN category does not correspond directly to these previously described bursting VIP-INs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of VIP-INs may exist along a continuum of active properties which only partially overlap with molecular markers and morphology.
source: It is possible that the electrophysiological properties of VIP-INs defined here do not constitute clearly delimited 'subtypes' per se, but rather exist along a continuum of active properties which only partially overlap with molecular markers (such as CR and CCK) and morphology.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: An irregular firing pattern that can be modulated by cholinergic suppression of M-current appears to be a durable feature of approximately 50% of VIP-INs.
source: Nevertheless, an irregular firing pattern that can be modulated by cholinergic suppression of M-current appears to be a durable feature of ~ 50% of VIP-INs.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the classification data in Figure 2 and cholinergic modulation data in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of Nav1.1 could have drastically different effects in IS vs. CA VIP-INs based on electrophysiological context, such as the overall level of M-current and the degree of reliance on Nav1.1.
source: The model illustrates how loss of Nav1.1 could have drastically different effects in IS vs. CA VIP-INs based on electrophysiological context, such as the overall level of M-current and the degree of reliance on Nav1.1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling shown in Figure 8.

claim: VIP-IN activity is important for the cortical state transition that occurs in response to cholinergic neuromodulation.
source: VIP-INs are recruited during shifts in attentional state, and their activity is important for the cortical state transition that occurs in response to cholinergic neuromodulation (Batista-Brito et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cholinergic input may enhance VIP-IN excitability during cortical state transitions by inhibiting M-current.
source: Our data suggest that cholinergic input may enhance VIP-IN excitability during cortical state transitions by inhibiting M-current.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the carbachol and muscarine experiments in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: IS VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice may play a particularly important role in the activity of IS VIP-INs during shifts in attentional state.
source: This effect may be important during shifts in attentional state, which are known to recruit VIP-IN activity. Our data also implies that IS VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice may play a particularly important role in the activity of IS VIP-INs during such state changes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the combination of cholinergic modulation data and IS VIP-IN dysfunction in Scn1a+/- mice.

claim: VIP-IN dysfunction may contribute to both the epilepsy and the severe cognitive impairments characteristic of Dravet syndrome.
source: Overall, our findings identify a novel cellular locus of dysfunction in Dravet Syndrome which may be relevant to both the epilepsy and the severe cognitive impairments characteristic of this disease.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Scn1a+/- mice on a 50:50 129S6:B6J background replicate the core phenotype of Dravet Syndrome.
source: All mice used for experiments were on a near 50:50 129S6:B6J background, and Scn1a+/- mice on this background have been shown to replicate the core phenotype of Dravet Syndrome (Miller et al., 2014; Mistry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work validating the mouse model.

claim: 32% of Scn1a.VIP-Cre.tdT mice died spontaneously by P55.
source: We observed similar rates of spontaneous death (17/52, or 32%, of Scn1a.VIP-Cre.tdT mice not used for experiments by P55; Favero et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the breeding colony.

claim: 100% of P21-50 Scn1a.VIP-Cre.tdT mice could be thermally induced to have seizures at or below 42°C core body temperature.
source: and were able to thermally induce seizures in 100% (9/9) of P21-50 Scn1a.VIP-Cre.tdT mice at or below 42°C core body temperature, supporting the validity of using these mice as a tool to study VIP-IN function in Dravet Syndrome.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from thermal seizure induction experiments.

claim: Dravet syndrome is characterized by temperature-sensitive and spontaneous seizures in the first year of life followed by progression to intractable epilepsy, intellectual disability with autistic features, and a markedly increased rate of sudden unexpected death (SUDEP).
source: Dravet syndrome (DS) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by temperature-sensitive and spontaneous seizures in the first year of life followed by progression to intractable epilepsy, intellectual disability with autistic features, and a markedly increased rate of sudden unexpected death (SUDEP) (Genton et al., 2011; Kalume et al., 2013; Oakley et al., 2009; Scheffer, 2012).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about Dravet syndrome supported by citations.

claim: DS is caused by pathogenic loss of function variants in the gene SCN1A, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the voltage gated sodium (Na+) channel α subunit Nav1.1.
source: DS is caused by pathogenic loss of function variants in the gene SCN1A, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the voltage gated sodium (Na+) channel α subunit Nav1.1 (Claes et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic cause of DS supported by citation.

claim: Experimental models of DS include mice lacking a functional copy of Nav1.1 (Scn1a+/- mice) and neurons generated from induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells derived from DS patients.
source: Experimental models of DS, including mice lacking a functional copy of Nav1.1 (Scn1a+/- mice) (Mistry et al., 2014; Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006) and neurons generated from induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells derived from DS patients (Liu et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2016), have provided important insights into the cellular and circuit basis of this disorder.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DS models supported by citations.

claim: DS remains incurable with a poor prognosis.
source: Despite advances in the understanding of underlying disease pathogenesis, DS remains incurable with a poor prognosis.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about DS.

claim: How loss of Nav1.1 leads to the features that define Dravet syndrome is incompletely understood.
source: How loss of Nav1.1 leads to the features that define this clinical syndrome is incompletely understood, and identifying new, targetable loci of dysfunction is critically important to developing new treatments.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.
